collections.surgeries.surgery_appendix.s: Incision and Entry through the Abdominal Wall

After the incision begins, the scrub nurse passes the instruments needed to enter the abdominal wall in sequence, the assistant surgeon maintains incision exposure, and the circulating nurse checks the lighting, suction, and records outside the sterile field. The skin, subcutaneous tissue, and abdominal wall layers are entered in sequence.
The abdominal wall layers have been entered. The team awaits Dr. Sakaguchi's confirmation to proceed.
Confirm entry through the abdominal wall and continue
“Understood. Continuing.”
Peritoneal Entry and Establishing the Right Lower Quadrant Surgical Field
After the peritoneum is entered, the assistant gradually adjusts retraction, bringing the ileocecal region into view.
How should the right lower quadrant surgical field be established next?
Adjust retraction first to obtain a clear right lower quadrant surgical field
“Understood. Continuing.”
Continue entry with the current exposure
“Understood. Continuing.”
Finding the Cecum and Locating the Appendix
The ileocecal region is exposed, and the team follows the anatomical relationships to find the appendix.
How should the appendix's location be confirmed?
Locate the appendix step by step using its relationship to the cecum
“Understood. Continuing.”
Look for the appendix directly within the current surgical field
“Understood. Continuing.”
“It's not as clear here as it looked a moment ago.”
Mobilizing and Fully Exposing the Appendix
The appendix has been found. The assistant maintains retraction as the surrounding tissue planes are gradually separated.
How should mobilization and exposure of the appendix proceed?
Mobilize and fully deliver the appendix before proceeding
“Understood. Continuing.”
Maintain the current exposure and work toward the mesoappendix during mobilization
“Understood. Continuing.”
“The surgical field is narrow. We'll need to be more careful as we proceed.”
Managing the Mesoappendix and Blood Supply
The appendix is fully exposed. Management of the mesoappendix and blood supply comes next.
Choose the pace of the procedure.
Cautious approach: control the mesoappendix in sections while maintaining a clear surgical field
“Understood. Continuing.”
Standard approach: manage the mesoappendix and blood supply at a normal pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Rapid approach: speed up management of the mesoappendix to reach the base sooner
“Understood. Continuing.”
“The current surgical field won't allow us to go any faster.”
Managing the Appendiceal Base
The mesoappendix and blood supply have been managed. The team turns to the appendiceal base.
How should control of the base be completed?
Reconfirm the anatomical relationships at the base before completing control
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete management of the base directly with the current surgical field
“Understood. Continuing.”
“We still need a clearer view of the anatomical relationships at the base.”
Removing the Appendix and Completing Stump Management
Management of the appendiceal base is complete. The specimen is about to leave the surgical field.
How should the team proceed to the final review after removal?
After removal, first tidy up the stump and surrounding surgical field
“Understood. Continuing.”
Proceed directly to the final review after removal
“Understood. Continuing.”
Correcting the Surgical Field
The main procedure is complete, but the surgical field still needs correction.
The current surgical field needs attention before the final review.
Reestablish exposure and perform additional hemostasis
“Understood. Continuing.”
Maintain the current situation and leave it for the final review
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Let's not put this off any longer.”
Final Review and Hemostasis
The appendix has been removed. The scrub nurse completes the specimen check, and the team begins inspecting the stump and surrounding surgical field.
How should the pre-closure review be completed?
Thoroughly review the stump, surrounding tissues, and hemostasis
“Understood. Continuing.”
Perform a focused review and close if the condition is acceptable
“Understood. Continuing.”
“There's still some oozing here.”
Closure
The final review is complete. The scrub nurse begins the final count, and the assistant helps close in layers.
Close the incision and end the operation.
Complete closure and end the operation
“Understood. Continuing.”

collections.surgeries.surgery_breast_tum: Incision and Entry into the Lesion Area
Incision and entry into the lesion area.

collections.surgeries.surgery_hysterecto: Laparotomy / Establishing the Pelvic Surgical Field

After entry into the abdominal cavity, {assistant_name} shifts the focus of retraction to the pelvis, while {scrub_name} organizes the retraction, dissection, and hemostatic instruments needed for the gynecological phase; {circulator_name} adjusts the lighting and records the time of entry into the main phase. The uterus and bilateral adnexa gradually come into view.
Confirm completion of the current stage.
Confirm entry into the pelvis and continue
“Understood. Continuing.”
Examining the Uterus / Adnexa / Adhesions and Mobility

{assistant_name} adjusts the uterus's position so that the uterine body, adnexa, and pelvic sidewalls can all be examined; {scrub_name} keeps dissection instruments ready. The team first assesses uterine size and mobility, and whether any adhesions will affect the subsequent approach.
Choose the next approach.
Thoroughly inspect the pelvic anatomical relationships and first address anything obstructing exposure
“Understood. Continuing.”
The current anatomical relationships are clear; proceed directly to uterine mobilization as planned
“Understood. Continuing.”
Round Ligament / Broad Ligament Approach

The uterus can now be held under stable traction. {assistant_name} maintains exposure on one side of the pelvis while {scrub_name} assists in opening the tissue planes leading into the broad ligament region; once complete, space gradually becomes available for the subsequent bladder dissection and vessel management.
Choose the next approach.
Fully open the tissue planes on both sides before proceeding deeper
“Understood. Continuing.”
Proceed to the next stage with the current exposure
“Understood. Continuing.”
Displacing the Bladder Inferiorly / Anterior Cervical Dissection

Once the lower uterus and anterior cervix enter the surgical field, {assistant_name} maintains upward traction on the uterus, gradually revealing the plane between the bladder and cervix; {scrub_name} assists with fine dissection and local hemostasis. Only when the bladder is truly clear of the planned resection area will there be enough space for the subsequent steps.
Choose the next approach.
Gradually displace the bladder inferiorly along clear tissue planes to fully expose the lower uterus
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete bladder mobilization at a normal pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Speed up bladder mobilization within the current tissue plane
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Managing the Adnexal Pedicles while Preserving the Ovaries

The bladder has been moved inferiorly. {assistant_name} exposes the connections between the upper uterus and adnexa in sequence; {scrub_name} prepares vascular control and hemostatic materials. As this operation preserves the ovaries by default, the team must keep the anatomical relationships on the preserved side clear while dividing the connections on the uterine side.
Choose the next approach.
Confirm the structures to be preserved on each side and control the pedicles step by step
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete management of the adnexal pedicles on the uterine side bilaterally at a normal pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Reduce intermediate adjustments and complete both sides quickly
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Confirming the Ureteral Course / Preparing the Uterine Vessels

Before managing the uterine vessels, {assistant_name} readjusts sidewall exposure so the ureteral course and uterine vessel region can be assessed together; {scrub_name} keeps vascular control instruments ready. Speed is not the objective at this stage; the aim is to clarify the anatomical relationships needed for the next step.
Choose the next approach.
Thoroughly confirm the pelvic sidewall anatomical relationships before managing the uterine vessels
“Understood. Continuing.”
The current anatomical relationships are clear; proceed to vascular control as planned
“Understood. Continuing.”
Uterine Vessel Control

The uterine vessels are now clearly visible. {assistant_name} maintains stable tension between the uterus and sidewall, while {scrub_name} continuously supplies instruments for vascular control and additional hemostasis; {circulator_name} keeps reserve materials readily available. The real risk of major bleeding is concentrated in this stage.
Choose the next approach.
Confirm and fully control the uterine vessels on each side
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete bilateral vascular control at a normal pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Reduce intermediate reviews to complete vessel management faster
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Managing the Cardinal / Uterosacral Ligament Support Structures

Once vascular control is secure, the uterus has noticeably lost its lateral attachments. {assistant_name} continues upward traction on the uterus, bringing the support tissues around the cervix into the operative area in sequence; {scrub_name} assists with dissection, hemostasis, and ligation. After this stage, only the final inferior connections of the uterus remain to be addressed.
Choose the next approach.
Keep the tissue planes around the cervix clear and manage the support structures step by step
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete management of the support structures around the cervix at a normal pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Speed up management of the support structures
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Completing the Circumferential Incision / Removing the Uterus

The tissues around the cervix are now fully accessible. After the final circumferential incision is completed, the uterus is removed from the pelvis. {scrub_name} receives the specimen and hands it to {circulator_name} for labeling outside the sterile field and documentation of submission for examination; {assistant_name} immediately reexposes the vaginal cuff and pelvic floor.
Confirm completion of the current stage.
Confirm removal of the uterus and proceed to vaginal cuff closure
“Understood. Continuing.”
Vaginal Cuff Closure / Restoring Pelvic Support

The uterus has left the surgical field. The open vaginal cuff must now be closed and stabilized. {assistant_name} controls tissue tension on both sides while {scrub_name} continuously passes sutures and hemostatic materials; as closure progresses, the pelvic floor gradually regains its integrity.
Choose the next approach.
Control tension, close the cuff step by step, and review thoroughly
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete vaginal cuff closure at a normal pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Shorten intermediate reviews to complete cuff closure as soon as possible
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Reexposing the Vaginal Cuff / Pelvis and Performing Additional Hemostasis

The main vaginal cuff closure is complete, but the current pelvic condition is still less than ideal. {assistant_name} reexposes the cuff and the areas of vascular management on both sides, while {scrub_name} prepares instruments for additional suturing, suction, and hemostasis; {circulator_name} records the time spent reworking and replenishes consumables.
Choose the next approach.
Fully reexpose the cuff and the treated areas on both sides, and complete additional hemostasis and reworking
“Understood. Continuing.”
Address only the areas most in need of adjustment and proceed to the final pelvic review as soon as possible
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Final Review of the Pelvis / Urinary Structures / Hemostasis

The main resection and closure are complete. {assistant_name} changes the retraction angle in sequence to bring the vaginal cuff, both sides of the pelvis, and the previously treated areas back into view; {scrub_name} assists with irrigation and final hemostasis. Before closing the abdominal wall, the team confirms that the pelvis is stable overall.
Choose the next approach.
Thoroughly review the vaginal cuff, both sides of the pelvis, and hemostasis
“Understood. Continuing.”
Focus the review on the current areas of risk and close the abdominal wall if the condition is acceptable
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Abdominal Wall Closure

Once the pelvis is confirmed stable, {scrub_name} completes the final count and passes closure materials, while {assistant_name} assists with closing the abdominal wall in layers; {circulator_name} completes the specimen, operative time, and postoperative transfer records.
Confirm completion of the current stage.
Complete closure and end the operation
“Understood. Continuing.”
With the pelvis exposed, the anatomical relationships of the uterus and bilateral adnexa are relatively clear, and uterine mobility is sufficient to begin mobilization as planned.
There are substantial pelvic adhesions and limited uterine mobility. The tissue planes on the bladder side and along the pelvic sidewalls are more crowded than in a routine case.
collections.surgeries.surgery_cabg.stage: Median Sternotomy / Exposing the Heart
The sternum has been opened, and the pericardial region is in the surgical field. Confirm entry into the main CABG phase.
Median sternotomy is complete, and the heart and ascending aorta are exposed.

After median sternotomy, `{assistant_name}` assists in establishing sternal retraction and exposing the pericardium, while `{scrub_name}` prepares cardiac retractors, suction, and vascular instruments in sequence; `{circulator_name}` coordinates the cardiopulmonary bypass equipment and documentation outside the sterile field. The heart and ascending aorta gradually enter the main surgical field.
Confirm sternotomy and exposure of the heart
“Understood. Continuing.”
Graft Preparation / LIMA and Backup Conduits
The bypass conduits are being prepared. How will you confirm their suitability?
LIMA / backup bypass graft preparation and assessment are complete.

`{assistant_name}` assists with exposure and preparation on the internal mammary artery side, while the peripheral harvesting team prepares the backup venous conduits; `{scrub_name}` keeps vascular clamps, irrigation, and suturing materials ready. Before cardiopulmonary bypass begins, the lead surgeon confirms the usable conduit lengths and their match to the targets.
Thoroughly review conduit length, course, and target matching
“Understood. Continuing.”
The current conduit conditions are clear; continue as planned
“Understood. Continuing.”
Confirming Coronary Targets / Bypass Sequence
The coronary targets are in view. Should the distal targets and bypass sequence be thoroughly confirmed first?
Coronary targets and the bypass sequence have been confirmed.

`{assistant_name}` adjusts the direction of cardiac exposure so the main coronary targets can be matched to the preoperative angiography plan; `{scrub_name}` prepares microvascular suturing materials and coronary instruments. Before cardiopulmonary bypass, the team makes one final confirmation of which graft connects where.
Confirm each distal target and the bypass sequence
“Understood. Continuing.”
They match the preoperative angiography plan; continue
“Understood. Continuing.”
Heparinization / Cannulation / Establishing Cardiopulmonary Bypass
The aortic and venous cannulation sites are prepared. How will you establish cardiopulmonary bypass?
Cannulation is complete, and cardiopulmonary bypass is established.

`{assistant_name}` maintains exposure of the ascending aorta and right side of the heart, while `{scrub_name}` passes cannulation and fixation materials in sequence; the perfusion team outside the sterile field connects the circuit. As cardiopulmonary bypass is established, the circulatory workload is gradually transferred to the pump-oxygenator system, and preparations begin for myocardial protection in the next phase.
Establish cannulation and cardiopulmonary bypass step by step, fully confirming stability
“Understood. Continuing.”
Establish cardiopulmonary bypass at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Reduce intermediate reviews to establish cardiopulmonary bypass as soon as possible
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Aortic Cross-Clamping / Myocardial Protection
Cardiopulmonary bypass is stable. How should aortic cross-clamping and myocardial protection be completed to obtain a still surgical field?
Aortic cross-clamping and myocardial protection are complete, providing a stable cardiac surgical field.

After aortic cross-clamping, cardioplegic solution enters the coronary system. `{assistant_name}` maintains exposure of the heart and aortic root, while `{scrub_name}` prepares coronary bypass instruments. The heart gradually stops beating, providing the lead surgeon with the stable field needed for precise anastomoses.
Thoroughly confirm cross-clamping and myocardial protection to obtain a stable surgical field
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete cross-clamping and myocardial protection at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete cross-clamping quickly and proceed to anastomosis
“Understood. Continuing.”
First Distal Coronary Anastomosis
The first target coronary artery is exposed. What pace will you use to complete the distal anastomosis?
The first distal coronary anastomosis is complete.

`{assistant_name}` stabilizes the local myocardium and maintains the orientation of the coronary incision, while `{scrub_name}` continuously passes fine vascular sutures and irrigation materials. The first distal anastomosis is both the technical core and the reference for the pace of the subsequent multiple bypasses.
Fully stabilize the target and check the first distal anastomosis stitch by stitch
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete the first distal anastomosis at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Reduce intermediate checks to complete the first distal anastomosis quickly
“Understood. Continuing.”
Additional Distal Bypasses
The first distal anastomosis is complete. How should the remaining planned targets be handled?
The remaining planned distal bypasses are complete.

The heart is repositioned through different exposure angles in sequence. `{assistant_name}` keeps each coronary target stable, while `{scrub_name}` changes conduits and sutures to match the lead surgeon's pace. The remaining distal grafts are gradually completed, giving each ischemic area scheduled for revascularization a new blood flow route.
Adjust exposure for each target and complete the additional distal grafts
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete the remaining distal anastomoses at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Maintain the current pace to complete the additional graft pathways quickly
“Understood. Continuing.”
Proximal Aortic Anastomoses / Completing the Graft Pathways
The distal grafts are established. How should the proximal anastomoses requiring connection to the ascending aorta be completed?
Proximal aortic anastomoses are complete, forming complete graft pathways.

`{assistant_name}` reestablishes exposure of the ascending aorta, while `{scrub_name}` prepares instruments for aortic-side anastomoses and materials for arranging the conduits. The proximal ends of the venous grafts are connected to the ascending aorta in sequence, and the full set of coronary bypasses begins to form complete inflow and outflow pathways.
Fully arrange the graft courses before completing each proximal anastomosis
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete the proximal anastomoses at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Reduce graft arrangement to complete the proximal connections quickly
“Understood. Continuing.”
Rewarming / Restoring the Heartbeat / Weaning from Cardiopulmonary Bypass
The main graft pathways are complete. How will you restore the heartbeat and wean from cardiopulmonary bypass?
The heartbeat has been restored, and weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass is complete.

After the aortic cross-clamp is released, myocardial perfusion resumes. `{assistant_name}` observes cardiac filling and contraction, while `{scrub_name}` keeps defibrillation, temporary pacing, and additional hemostatic instruments ready; perfusion flow is gradually returned to the patient's own circulation.
Restore the heartbeat in stages and cautiously wean from cardiopulmonary bypass
“Understood. Continuing.”
Rewarm, restore the heartbeat, and wean from bypass at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Wean from bypass as soon as possible, reducing intermediate adjustments
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Reviewing Graft Flow / Anastomoses / Hemostasis
The heart has resumed its own circulation. Should each graft's flow and anastomoses be thoroughly reviewed?
Graft flow, anastomoses, and mediastinal hemostasis have been reviewed.

`{assistant_name}` assists in exposing the distal and proximal anastomotic regions in sequence, while `{scrub_name}` helps check for oozing and prepares additional sutures. The team confirms that each graft follows a natural course with reliable flow, and that no new problems have emerged as the heart resumes beating.
Thoroughly review the flow and anastomoses of each graft
“Understood. Continuing.”
Focus the review on high-risk anastomoses
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Reexposing Grafts / Anastomoses
The graft or anastomotic condition requires reworking. How will you address it?
The problematic graft has been reexposed, and the necessary revisions are complete.

Flow through one graft or the condition of an anastomosis is less than ideal. `{assistant_name}` reestablishes exposure of the corresponding area, while `{scrub_name}` prepares additional vascular sutures and irrigation materials; the team outside the sterile field records the additional cardiopulmonary bypass / revision time.
Reexpose the problematic graft and revise its flow / anastomosis
“Understood. Continuing.”
Revise only the most obvious problem and finish reworking as soon as possible
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Decannulation / Mediastinal Drainage / Final Hemostasis
Circulation is stable. Complete decannulation and preparations for closure.
Cardiopulmonary bypass cannulas have been removed, and mediastinal drainage and final hemostasis preparations are complete.

After confirming that a return to cardiopulmonary bypass is unnecessary, the cannulas are removed gradually and the cannulation sites are treated. `{scrub_name}` completes preparations for mediastinal drainage and the final instrument count, while `{assistant_name}` continues reviewing cardiac and mediastinal hemostasis; `{circulator_name}` records the final circulatory phase.
Confirm completion of the current stage
“Understood. Continuing.”
Sternal Closure
The mediastinal condition is stable. Complete sternal and chest wall closure to end the operation.
Sternal and chest wall closure is complete.

Once drainage and hemostasis are confirmed, `{scrub_name}` passes sternal fixation and layered closure materials, while `{assistant_name}` helps restore the chest wall layers; `{circulator_name}` completes preparations for postoperative transfer to the ICU.
Confirm completion of the current stage
“Understood. Continuing.”
collections.surgeries.surgery_cabg.case_: The coronary targets are small, and the disease is relatively diffuse. The plan remains feasible, but each distal anastomosis depends more heavily on stable exposure and patience.
collections.surgeries.surgery_explorator: Midline Laparotomy / Establishing Access to the Entire Abdominal Cavity
The abdominal cavity is open. Confirm entry into systematic exploration.
Midline laparotomy is complete, with access established for exploration of the entire abdominal cavity.

After the midline incision is established, {assistant_name} helps widen exposure of the upper and lower abdomen, while {scrub_name} passes long-handled retractors, suction, and basic hemostatic instruments; {circulator_name} adjusts the lighting and records the start time of exploration.
Confirm access to the entire abdominal cavity and begin exploration
“Understood. Continuing.”
Rapid Overall Inspection / Setting Priorities
The abdominal cavity is fully open. Should an overall inspection be performed before exploring by region?
The overall abdominal survey is complete, and priorities for systematic exploration are confirmed.

{assistant_name} changes the direction of retraction in sequence to bring the subdiaphragmatic region, upper abdomen, bowel, and pelvic inlet quickly into view; {scrub_name} keeps suction and hemostatic instruments ready.
Complete an overall survey first and mark suspicious areas
“Understood. Continuing.”
There is no urgent problem at present; proceed directly to systematic exploration
“Understood. Continuing.”
Systematic Upper Abdominal Exploration
Upper abdominal exploration begins. How will you examine the liver, spleen, stomach, and deep upper abdominal structures?
Systematic exploration of the major upper abdominal organs and deep regions is complete.
{assistant_name} lifts the liver edge, stomach, and perisplenic region in sequence, while {scrub_name} assists with suction, gauze, and long-handled dissection instruments.
Expose the upper abdomen region by region, ensuring that every deep region is truly visible
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete systematic upper abdominal exploration in the standard sequence
“Understood. Continuing.”
Reduce repositioning of retractors between regions to finish the upper abdominal examination quickly
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Segment-by-Segment Small Bowel Exploration
The small bowel needs a complete examination from proximal to distal. What pace will you use?
A systematic examination of the small bowel from proximal to distal is complete.
{assistant_name} passes and spreads out the small bowel segment by segment, while {scrub_name} keeps moist gauze and suction ready.
Spread out each segment from proximal to distal and examine both surfaces and the mesenteric side
“Understood. Continuing.”
Examine the entire small bowel at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Keep the bowel moving continuously and reduce pauses for a quick examination
“Understood. Continuing.”
Exploring the Colon / Mesentery / Lateral Abdomen
The small bowel examination is complete. How should the colon, mesentery, and both sides of the abdomen be examined next?
Exploration of the colon, mesentery, and both sides of the abdomen is complete.

{assistant_name} exposes the right colon, transverse colon, left colon, and main mesenteric regions in sequence, while {scrub_name} switches suction and retraction instruments as the surgical field changes.
Expose the colon, mesentery, and concealed lateral abdominal areas segment by segment
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete examination of the colon and mesentery in the standard sequence
“Understood. Continuing.”
Pause only at clearly suspicious sites and examine the remaining regions quickly
“Understood. Continuing.”
Exploring the Pelvis / Lower Abdomen / Retroperitoneal Region
The main bowel segments in the abdominal cavity have been examined. How will you approach the pelvis and retroperitoneal region?
Exploration of the pelvis, lower abdomen, and retroperitoneal region is complete.

{assistant_name} gathers the bowel toward the upper abdomen, gradually bringing the pelvis, lower abdomen, and suspicious retroperitoneal areas into view; {scrub_name} prepares deep retractors and suction.
Rearrange the bowel to fully expose the pelvis and retroperitoneal region
“Understood. Continuing.”
Complete pelvic / retroperitoneal exploration at a standard pace
“Understood. Continuing.”
Maintain the current retraction and quickly examine the deep regions
“Understood. Continuing.”
Targeted Reexamination of Suspicious Areas
After systematic exploration, one area still does not fully agree with the imaging, symptoms, or intraoperative observations. How will you reexamine it?
Targeted reexamination of the main suspicious / inconsistent area is complete.
{assistant_name} once again establishes the best angle for the suspicious area, while {scrub_name} prepares suction, irrigation, and any necessary instruments for local treatment.
Reestablish the best angle and fully account for the suspicious area
“Understood. Continuing.”
Perform a targeted reexamination based on the current clues
“Understood. Continuing.”
“Please confirm once more.”
Confirm only the most direct explanation without broadening the reexamination

Exploration Findings / Completeness Review
The main regions have been examined. Should a checklist be used to confirm that no areas have been missed before ending exploration?

{assistant_name} recites the abdominal regions already examined in the prescribed sequence, while {scrub_name} completes preparations for local irrigation; {circulator_name} records the key findings.

{assistant_name} repositions the bowel and retractors to restore the view of the corresponding region; {scrub_name} prepares additional suction, irrigation, and materials for local treatment.

Final Irrigation / Hemostasis / Review of the Entire Abdomen
The exploration findings are clear. Complete the final tidying of the surgical field.
Final irrigation, hemostasis, and review of the entire abdomen are complete.

{assistant_name} makes one final check that there are no new sites of bleeding or contamination in the abdominal cavity, while {scrub_name} completes irrigation, suction, and preparations for the instrument count.
Confirm completion of the current stage
“Understood. Continuing.”
Abdominal Wall Closure
The abdominal condition is stable. Complete abdominal wall closure.
Abdominal wall closure is complete.

{scrub_name} passes materials for layered closure, while {assistant_name} helps restore the abdominal wall layer by layer; {circulator_name} completes final documentation and preparations for postoperative transfer.

There are substantial preexisting adhesions and tissue obstructions within the abdomen, and several regions cannot be fully exposed in a single attempt. The real challenge is not opening the abdominal cavity, but ensuring that poor exposure does not cause any regions to be missed during systematic exploration.
